newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Red Cross mission chief sees wider Colombian role.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross mission chief sees wider Colombian role.

text.p: The Red Cross' central role in the release of government troops by leftist rebels could enable it to do more in trying to end Colombia's long war, a Red Cross official said on Sunday.

Pierre Gassmann, head of the Colombia mission of the International Committee of the Red Cross, described as intricate the negotiations that resulted in the handover on Sunday of 60 soldiers and 10 marines.
But he said the process had boosted the image of the Red Cross in a country where it has traditionally come under suspicion from both the left and the right.
"What we have now established is a better working relationship here, and that will help us pursue our role of helping those in the armed conflict to observe certain rules," Gassmann told Reuters.
"The government and civil society has seen us work, and they have a tool here which they can use in the future for dialogue with the guerrilla," he added.
The internal war in Colombia is the longest-running in Latin America. It has its roots in a 10-year civil war that started in the late 1940s and was known simply as the Violence.

Last August, in an incident considered one of the bloodiest in the entire conflict, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) seized 60 soldiers and killed some 30 others in a devastating attack in the southern province of Putumayo.
The seizure led to calls for renewing peace talks between the government and the FARC, which was set up as a pro-Soviet guerrilla force in 1964. The talks had collapsed without result in 1984.
The situation also led to comparisons with the recent Peruvian hostage crisis, sparked when fighters of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the Japanese embassy residence in Lima.
In contrast to the MRTA's VIP hostages, the Colombian servicemen, mostly from peasant backgrounds, were largely forgotten by the outside world.

The end of the crises presented a further contrast. In Peru there was savage criticism of the role played by the Red Cross, whom some accused of helping President Alberto Fujimori's government plan the bloody counterattack that left all the hostage-takers dead.
"The difference here is that nobody tried to win by force," Gassmann said.

To make way for the FARC to hand over the captive troops, the ICRC helped broker a deal that saw President Ernesto Samper order the army to pull out of a 5,000-square-mile (13,000 sq km) swathe of jungle in southern Colombia's Caqueta province for 32 days.

In the final stages, the organisation took strict control of the logistics of flying the 70 hostages from the jungle into Cartagena del Chaira aboard Russian-built helicopters loaned by the army and then on to Larandia, a military base outside the neutral zone.
In the early stages, the Swiss-based committee was the first point of contact between the guerrillas and the government. "We were the letterbox," Gassmann said.
